source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh)
finding: Lakatos names six methods for handling a counterexample: surrender, monster-barring, exception-barring, monster-adjusting, lemma-incorporation, and proofs-and-refutations. The first is the naive Popper reaction. The others repair concepts, the claim, or the proof.
numbers: Six methods. Lakatos gives surrender about 1 of 120 pages in the book (thesis ch. 11). Three are called main: monster-barring (concept), exception-barring (claim), proofs-and-refutations (proof).
limits: Thesis is a reading of Lakatos by Pease, not Lakatos himself. Monster-adjusting was left unimplemented.
agent_relevance: Our schema has only one reaction to a failed check: revise (S5). Lakatos gives a menu of typed reactions: drop, redefine terms, restrict claim, fix proof step. A repair-type slot is a candidate addition.

source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh)
finding: Core Lakatos classification. A global counterexample refutes the conclusion. A local counterexample refutes one proof step (lemma). A counterexample can be global only, local only, or both. Each type calls for a different repair.
numbers: Three cases: both global and local -> add the failing lemma as an explicit condition of the claim. Local only -> fix that proof step, keep the claim. Global only -> hunt for a hidden assumption in the proof, then make it explicit in proof and claim.
quote: If it is both global and local, then one should modify the conjecture by incorporating the problematic proof step as a condition.
limits: Needs a proof split into explicit steps that can each be tested. Works for informal proofs only if the steps are written down.
agent_relevance: Maps to S5 REVISE. Code can classify a failing test by running it against the claim and against each stated step. Answers SUBFIELDS question (a) in principle: the classifier needs a stepwise solution trace with a checkable claim per step.

source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh)
finding: Pease turned the type test into Algorithm 8. If a global counterexample also breaks a lemma, do global-and-local incorporation. Else if some lemma has a local counterexample and a concept in the theory links the local and global counterexample and appears in a lemma, do global-and-local incorporation. Else do hidden-lemma incorporation. No global but a local counterexample: local-only. None: return unchanged.
numbers: One decision procedure, four outcomes (global+local, hidden-lemma, local-only, unchanged). The linking-concept test exists to stop confusing a hidden-lemma case with a global+local case.
limits: Run in HRL on toy cases only (left-cancellation law for groupoids; Hilbert betweenness theorem; Lakatos cylinder). No benchmark of correct classification rates.
agent_relevance: A ready-made, code-checkable branching rule for revise. The hard part is the hidden-lemma branch, which needs a notion of surprise.

source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh)
finding: Hidden-lemma search is the hardest method to implement. Pease defines two kinds of surprise to locate the hidden assumption. Type 1: entity x is the only counterexample to a stronger conjecture (P and Q and R) for some concept R. Type 2: x is outside the antecedent, not P(x), so the claim is about a meaningless term (circle as a polygon).
numbers: Two surprise tests. Type 1 uses HR's record of each concept's construction path (ancestors) to dissect the conclusion concept until the missing condition R appears.
quote: an entity x is surprising with respect to a conjecture P -> Q if there exists another conjecture C such that x is the only counterexample
limits: Type 2 handles only one-argument predicates; the author calls it a simplification of Lakatos's circle example.
agent_relevance: A concrete rule for finding the missing condition: look for a property that every other example has and the counterexample alone lacks. Can be run in code by testing candidate predicates against the example set (G3 held-out check still needed).

source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh)
finding: Monster-barring keeps the claim and changes the meaning of its terms. The object is excluded as not really a case of the concept. Example: hollow cube (V-E+F = 16-24+12 = 4) barred by defining polyhedron as a surface of polygons, not a solid. Pease lists reasons to bar: defend the claim, attack it, the object breaks many conjectures, or it turns other objects into counterexamples.
numbers: Hollow cube V-E+F=4 vs the claim V-E+F=2. Two decision points: whether to propose barring an object and how to answer the proposal.
limits: Danger noted by Lakatos and Pease: monster-barring can protect a claim by definition games. It is a repair that changes what the claim says.
agent_relevance: In an LLM loop, saying the counterexample is outside the problem's intended domain is a monster-barring move. It should be allowed only when the redefinition is stated explicitly and kept as a condition in the answer; otherwise it is silent claim-shrinking (G3 risk).

source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh)
finding: Exception-barring changes the claim, not the terms. Piecemeal exclusion generalises a counterexample into a class and excludes it (hollow cube -> polyhedra with cavities -> claim for polyhedra without cavities). Strategic withdrawal is the only method that uses positive examples: generalise from supporting cases (regular -> convex polyhedra) and restrict the claim to that class.
numbers: Euler example: V-E+F = 2 restricted to convex polyhedra, or to polyhedra without cavities.
limits: Restriction can over-shrink: Pease notes over-modified claims become dull or too specific, so a stop rule is needed.
agent_relevance: The two restriction operators for a failed general rule: exclude the failing class, or keep only the class the examples support. Both are code-checkable on held-out cases. An over-restriction stop rule is a G7/G12 style budget.

source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh)
finding: HRL system design. Each agent is a copy of the HR theory-formation program with its own slice of the data. There are students and one teacher. Work alternates between independent work phases and a discussion phase. Students exchange conjectures, concepts, proof schemes and counterexamples, then keep what passes an interestingness threshold.
numbers: Default 2 students; experiments used 3 students, 10 independent phases, 20 theory-formation steps per phase. Interestingness = weighted sum of surprisingness, comprehensibility, applicability, plausibility (0.5 each by default; 3 on one measure for the animal students).
limits: Data split across agents is what creates disagreement; with one agent holding all the data there is nothing to refute. Message order is non-deterministic.
agent_relevance: Disagreement between differently informed copies is the engine of refutation here. This sits close to G4/G9: our rules say agreeing samples are not evidence and debate does not beat voting. The Lakatos agents differ in data, not only in persona, and counterexamples are checked by code.

source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh)
finding: Surrender experiments (HRL, five rules for when to give up a conjecture). 42 sessions: 14 each in group theory, animal taxonomy, number theory, 3 students each. The best single rule was the interestingness threshold (only rule whose results were all in the desirable quadrants), then comparing a conjecture's interestingness to the theory average. Modification-count 0 (surrender at first counterexample) was surprisingly one of the best; count 3 was worst (everything modified, mostly uninteresting).
numbers: 42 sessions (14 x 3 domains). Five variables: number of prior modifications (0-3), interestingness threshold (0.5, 0.75, 1.0), compare to average, plausibility threshold (0.7-0.9), domain-of-application threshold (0.4-0.8).
limits: Judged by the agents' own interestingness scores, not an external measure, so partly circular. Author says threshold values were inconclusive.
agent_relevance: Evidence that revise-every-failure is bad: with a low-value claim, giving up is as good as repairing. Supports a repair budget and a value check before repair in S5/S6.

source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh)
finding: Monster-barring experiments. When agents were asked which object to propose as a monster, correctness was 82-100% in group theory (odd algebras GP2, GP3, SG1), 94-100% on the animal set (platypus), and 97% in number theory (0 and 1). It found the platypus and the numbers 0 and 1 as monsters. Reaction to proposals was worse: 82-88% correct in sessions 69-75 (group theory).
numbers: Table 10.8: group theory 82-100%, animals 94-100%, number theory 97%. Sessions 69-92 (all students able to propose): group theory 82-88%. A monster-barring minimum near 10% (share of the agent's conjectures an object must break) gave the most interesting behaviour.
limits: Ground truth is the author's own choice of which objects are odd. Semigroup SG1 was never proposed because it did not arise as a counterexample before the session ended. Numbers 2 and 3 were wrongly barred in one session.
agent_relevance: Fraction-of-conjectures-broken is a cheap, code-computable score for whether a counterexample is a monster or a real exception: an object that breaks many beliefs at once is probably outside the domain.

source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh)
finding: Monster-barring in vague-to-specific mode produced candidate definitions. In group theory the invented definitions resembled the group axioms: associativity was added to exclude groupoid GP2, and an inverse condition to exclude semigroup SG1. In number theory a definition requiring a|a excluded zero.
numbers: Definitions 1-5 (group theory) were the most satisfactory; 8-11 (number theory) were obscure and tied to how divisors were computed.
limits: Toy domains; definitions emerge from the program's own concept encoding.
agent_relevance: Shows counterexample-generated concepts can be produced mechanically: the definition is the smallest predicate that separates the counterexample from the rest. Compare Library learning and Schema induction subfields.

source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh)
finding: Exception-barring experiments in three domains. Piecemeal exclusion worked best in group theory, so HRL was not tuned only to number theory. Giving some but not all agents counterexample-barring seemed to improve modifications. The number of modifications was too small to fix parameters.
numbers: Table 10.17: number theory claim (a integer, a|a, a*a=a) modified to exclude a=1: surprisingness 1/61, plausibility 1, average interestingness 0.508 by counterexample-barring; another number theory modification by piecemeal exclusion scored 0.016. Group theory modifications ranged from 0 to 0.941 (17 groups). Animal set 18 animals, first modification 0.528.
limits: Few modifications per session, so no conclusions on optimal parameters. Preliminary.
agent_relevance: Numbers show that how a counterexample is generalised matters a lot (0.508 vs 0.016 on modifications of similar claims). The generalisation step is the point to check with held-out data.

source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh)
finding: Theorem Modifier (TM), a spin-off by Colton and Pease, automates exception-barring for algebra. Otter tries to prove the claim, then its negation. MACE builds supporting and falsifying models. HR invents specialisation concepts true of the supporting models; each is added as a condition and re-proved by Otter. Only proved modifications are shown.
numbers: TPTP test: 98 invented non-theorems -> valid modifications for 83%, average 3.1 modifications each. 9 real non-theorems from TPTP -> 7 repaired (78%). Settings: Otter and MACE 10 s, HR 3000 steps. Example RNG031-6 (rings).
limits: Non-theorems were made by deleting axioms or changing quantifiers, variables, bracketing, so repairs may just undo the corruption. Limited to algebra. Thesis footnote says this was joint Colton and Pease work.
agent_relevance: The closest measured result to a conjecture-refinement loop: a false claim is turned into a proved one by adding a condition that a prover then verifies. The verify-after-repair step is what makes it safe (G2, G3).

source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh)
finding: Evaluation was weak by modern standards. Chapter 10 tests only whether parameters change behaviour and whether outputs look interesting by the program's own measures. Chapter 11 argues by philosophical criteria (consilience, simplicity, Sloman's list). Lemma-incorporation had no hypothesis testing, only worked examples.
numbers: Three hypotheses (fine-tune surrender, monster-barring, exception-barring); 3 domains. No comparison to a baseline without Lakatos methods.
limits: No ablation against plain conjecturing; no external judge of interestingness; the author calls the tests preliminary.
agent_relevance: There is no measured evidence in the founding model that Lakatos-style repair beats simpler baselines. SUBFIELDS question (c) remains open and must be tested by us at equal tokens.

source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh)
finding: Feferman's ten criticisms of Lakatos (1978): what happened before 1847; is the method only for transitional periods; relation to working experience; is there no end to guessing; what counts as proof improvement; where does the first proof come from; form of conjectures; can ordinary logic explain the same cases; are there no crystal-clear concepts; what is distinctive about mathematics. Also Hacking (1981): the method is tied to hypothetico-deductive style.
numbers: Ten criticisms. Lakatos used essentially two case studies (Euler polyhedron formula, uniform convergence).
limits: Pease's answers are partial: the program needs an initial proof scheme given by hand, which leaves criticism (vi) open.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for our use: the method needs an initial proof or solution trace and a testable claim. Where there is no first attempt, Lakatos gives no help (see S3 GENERATE).

source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh)
finding: Lakatos himself did not claim a single logic of discovery (the editors added the subtitle). Popper's naive falsification says reject a refuted claim; Lakatos treats that as the weakest, first method. Counterexamples are used to refine claim, concept and proof instead.
numbers: Surrender takes about 1 of 120 pages.
limits: Secondary reading via Larvor (1998) as quoted in the thesis.
agent_relevance: Matches G1/G2 spirit: a failure is information about which part to repair, not only a signal to resample.

source: Martin and Pease (2013) Mathematical practice, crowdsourcing, and social machines
finding: Empirical check of Lakatos in real online maths talk. In a sample of mathoverflow questions, 34% of responses gave explicit examples or counterexamples to conjectures, a corrected error appeared in 37% of the sample, 56% cited literature. 90% of questions got a flagged answer; 78% reasonable, 12% partial.
numbers: mathoverflow: 34% examples/counterexamples, 37% corrected errors, 56% citations, 90% answered (78% reasonable + 12% partial).
limits: Sample size not stated in the part read. Informal coding by the authors; house rules shape the talk and little concept-formation was seen.
agent_relevance: Errors are accepted and corrected in a low-ego way. Counterexamples are a main currency of progress in real practice, supporting a counterexample-first revise step.

source: Martin and Pease (2013) Mathematical practice, crowdsourcing, and social machines
finding: Third mini-polymath, 174 comments coded by main activity: examples/counterexamples 33%, conjectures 20%, proofs 14%, concepts 10%, other 23%. A misleading word (windmill read as a half-line) produced counterexamples that exposed two readings of the concept: this is Lakatos's monster-adjusting.
numbers: 174 comments: 33% examples, 20% conjecture, 14% proof, 10% concept, 23% other.
limits: One problem, a simple geometry puzzle with a known solution. Authors say most examples fit Lakatos categories only with sufficient ingenuity; the fit is subtle and context-dependent.
agent_relevance: A failure case for any typed classifier: one object was a supporting example for one person and a counterexample for another. Code cannot settle that; it needs a restatement step (S1 UNDERSTAND) to fix the reading first.

source: Martin and Pease (2013) Mathematical practice, crowdsourcing, and social machines
finding: Authors say Lakatos explains how to repair a flawed assumption but not how it arises. They hypothesise that naming causes misconceptions (the word windmill suggested a pivoting half-line). Lakatos's picture was social but not necessarily collaborative.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: A hypothesis, not tested.
agent_relevance: The cause of an error can be a wrong reading of a term, so repair may need a re-read of the problem statement before changing the answer.

source: Werndl (2009) Justifying Definitions in Mathematics - Going Beyond Lakatos
finding: Lakatos's proof-generated definitions (a definition justified because the proof needs it) are only one way definitions get justified. From ergodic theory (randomness), Werndl finds three more: natural-world, condition and redundancy justification. Some definitions are both preformal-justified and proof-generated (Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy).
numbers: Four kinds of justification in total. One case-study field (ergodic theory).
limits: Single case study; philosophical argument, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Limits the claim that proof-generated concepts are the main source of new concepts. Concept creation also comes from a real-world meaning or a needed condition.

source: Li et al. (2025) One Example Shown, Many Concepts Known: COUNTERMATH (ICML 2025)
finding: Benchmark of 1,216 university-level statement-rationale pairs where the proof is a counterexample, from four textbook fields (algebra, topology, real analysis, functional analysis). Most statements are labelled True, since textbooks state correct claims. Judgement is scored by macro-F1; example use is scored by a GPT-4o judge.
numbers: 1,216 items. Judge example-extraction accuracy 97% as reported. Open 7B models score F1 around 30; Qwen2.5-Math-72B-Instruct 41.8; GPT-4o about 59.0 and o1-preview about 60.1; DeepSeek-R1 80.7.
limits: Table text was garbled in extraction so per-row values for commercial models are approximate. LLM judge for example quality. Label skew toward True.
agent_relevance: Models are weak at finding counterexamples even when they can judge truth. This bounds any loop that depends on the model to propose its own counterexample; a code-run search or tool should supply it (G2, G10).

source: Li et al. (2025) One Example Shown, Many Concepts Known: COUNTERMATH (ICML 2025)
finding: Fine-tuning on 1,025 counterexample-use samples lifted a 7B math model slightly. Base Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct F1 38.3, examples used 74.2%, strict 30.2%. After SFT: F1 41.1, examples 79.4%, strict 31.1%. The tuned model also scored higher on other benchmarks (for example AIME 2024 20.0 -> 30.0, MATH 80.5 -> 87.9).
numbers: 1,025 training samples. F1 38.3 -> 41.1 (+2.8). Strict 30.2 -> 31.1. Out-of-distribution row mapping read from a garbled table.
limits: Single model, single run, no seeds. The transfer numbers come from a flattened table and the row labels are uncertain. Later work (SymCE) shows counterexample-only SFT can damage truth recognition.
agent_relevance: Small gain from counterexample training; training is out of scope for our scaffold, so mainly a bound on what the model alone offers.

source: Sinha et al. (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? REFUTE benchmark
finding: REFUTE asks a model to create an input that makes a subtly wrong competitive-programming solution fail, checked by running code. The best reasoning agent, o3-mini (high) with code-execution feedback, makes a valid counterexample for under 9% of wrong submissions, though it can solve up to about 48% of the same problems.
numbers: 324 samples by 304 authors. o3-mini (high) RandSearch 8.3%; with the correct solution given (oracle) 15.1% for DeepSeek-V3 and 9.9% for DeepSeek-R1. Median 17 test cases passed by each wrong submission. Of failed RandSearch runs, 35% end in a wrong counterexample; 86% of those from wrong brute-force code.
limits: Competitive programming only. Other models scored roughly 2% to 6% in the prompting table (garbled in extraction).
agent_relevance: Solving is much easier than falsifying. Even handing the model the correct answer helps little. Strong support for letting code, not the model, generate and check counterexamples, and for not trusting a model's report of no counterexample found.

source: Zouak et al. (2026) Counterexample Generation via Per-Theorem Symbolic Verifiers (SymCE)
finding: Counterexamples built by dropping a hypothesis from a true theorem (exception-barring in reverse). A Python verifier per theorem scores a witness. Qwen3-4B on 201 held-out items: greedy pass@1 base 0.30, SFT 0.35, RL with verifier reward 0.50 (4-seed means 0.49 dense, 0.46 sparse). Best open 7B (Eurus-2-7B-PRIME) 0.30; frontier APIs 0.42-0.58.
numbers: Corpus 4,707 false conjectures from 6,748 theorems; verifier audit 173/177 = 97.7%. Pass@8: base 0.49, RL 0.68. Paired delta RL vs base +0.199 [0.13, 0.27]. SFT delta CI [-0.030, +0.119] (not significant).
limits: Undergraduate algebra and analysis only; a verifier per theorem was generated by tooling; 4B model; 2026 preprint, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: A counterexample is a witness that keeps every remaining premise and breaks the conclusion. That is exactly the local/global type test: code can score which premise a witness breaks. Verifier rewards, not text imitation, improved the skill.

source: Zouak et al. (2026) Counterexample Generation via Per-Theorem Symbolic Verifiers (SymCE)
finding: Imitation trap: training only on counterexamples makes the model call true theorems false. Recognition of true theorems fell from 0.27 to 0.00 after counterexample-only SFT (truth-classify prompt 0.36 -> 0.21); the SFT model asserted FALSE on 70% of true theorems. RL with a sparse outcome reward restored it to 0.65 (0.84 on truth-classify); dense partial credit only 0.34.
numbers: Truth probe n=347. Base 0.27/0.36, SFT 0.00/0.21, RL dense 0.34/0.73, RL sparse 0.65/0.84. Dense vs sparse gap 33 +- 8 points over four seeds. Collapse seen in four seeds and on Gemma-3-4B. Base gave no verdict on 62% of items.
limits: Single task family; the calibration probe shares format with training. Authors restrict the sparse-over-dense claim to that probe.
agent_relevance: A refutation drive without a guard creates false refutations. The loop needs a path where the claim may be true: a failed search for a counterexample must leave the claim standing (G3, G6).

source: Li et al. (2026) Learning to Disprove: Formal Counterexample Generation with LLMs
finding: Symbolic mutation: take a proved Lean 4 theorem, drop hypotheses unused in its proof, and ask the model for a formal counterexample. About 575K candidate problems from 212,463 seed theorems (mutation ratio 1.6-2.5, 0.3-0.71 s per theorem). The fine-tuned model solves more than the best baseline on three benchmarks, a relative pass@1 gain of 47% to 74%.
numbers: Seeds 212,463; mutated 575,039. FOR-COUNTER 1,058 formalised COUNTERMATH problems. Pass@1 counts, ours vs next best: 222 vs 127; 213 vs 144; 174 vs 111 (about +95, +69, +63 problems over the strongest baseline per the text).
limits: Marked Rejected from ICLR 2026. Counts, not rates, because the benchmark has known errors. Autoformalised benchmark. Table cells were garbled in extraction so baseline pairings are approximate.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis-dropping is a machine version of lemma-incorporation in reverse: an unused premise is exactly a candidate hidden lemma. Verification by Lean is the external check.

source: Ke et al. (2026) Towards Solving the Gilbert-Pollak Conjecture via Large Language Models
finding: LLMs write geometric lemmas as executable code; a verification function built from the lemmas certifies a lower bound for the Steiner ratio. Progressive lemma refinement driven by reflection on bottleneck regions raised the certified bound from 0.824 (stalled for about three decades) to 0.8559, with thousands of LLM calls.
numbers: Old bound 0.824, new 0.8559, conjectured value 0.866. Thousands of LLM calls.
limits: A proof-search system, not a Lakatos replication. Authors say scalar-reward-only refinement is insufficient; the reflection mechanism gives the model structured failure information. Preprint (v3, 2026).
agent_relevance: A measured case where lemma-level repair, checked by code, produced a new certified result. The lemma is repaired from where the bound fails, not from the model's opinion (G2).

source: Chuharski et al. (2024) Mining Math Conjectures from LLMs: A Pruning Approach
finding: Claude, Gemini 1.5 and GPT-4 generated conjectures about the solubilizer in group theory and wrote GAP code to test them on groups, pruning those with counterexamples. Of 757 outputs there were 420 unique conjectures; counterexamples were found for 109 (25.95%); only 40 (9.52%) survived with no counterexample; none was groundbreaking, and one rediscovered a published theorem that was in the prompt.
numbers: 757 outputs -> 420 unique. Survivors by model: GPT-4 26.60%, Gemini 4.64%, Claude 4.49%. Non-executable code in 271 cases (64.52%): Gemini 81.86%, Claude 49.44%, GPT-4 37.76%.
limits: Tiny scale, one narrow topic, one-shot prune, no refinement of survivors. Surviving GPT-4 conjectures were qualitatively more obvious (about set size). Survival only means no counterexample on the groups tried.
agent_relevance: Conjecture, test, prune works but most conjectures fail the test and code failures dominate. A pass here is not proof (G3): the groups tested must be held out from the ones that inspired the claim.

source: Lectures on AI for Mathematics (2026)
finding: Describes an iterative counterexample loop: a generator proposes a candidate counterexample, a verifier judges it and gives a specific reason for failure, and the generator revises using that feedback and the attempt history.
numbers: No measured results in the part read (a workflow description around line 6483 of the extracted text).
limits: Only the loop description was read, not the whole 600K-character document. Not Lakatos-specific.
agent_relevance: Same loop as our S4 TEST -> S5 REVISE, with the failure reason supplied by a checker. Matches G2.

source: Pease, Lawrence, Budzynska, Corneli, Reed (2017) Lakatos-style collaborative mathematics through dialectical, structured and abstract argumentation, Artificial Intelligence 246
finding: From the abstract page only: Lakatos's informal logic is read as a dialogue game over structured arguments; abstract argumentation semantics label which arguments are acceptable; the output is a current proof artefact viewable with its history, demonstrated on a real collaborative example. Full text was not readable (publisher blocked download).
numbers: No figures read.
limits: Abstract only; the PDF returned 403 and a bot check. Treat detail as unverified.
agent_relevance: Possible source for a move vocabulary (claim, counterexample, definition challenge) and for keeping revision history; check in angle B or a later pass.
